target.title: fix(validation): disable implicit pnpm installs
target.body:
## Summary

- disable pnpm's `verifyDepsBeforeRun` behavior for validation commands
- keep the existing lifecycle-hook suppression and workspace filter fail-closed behavior
- update focused command-boundary assertions

## Root cause

Dependency setup and validation intentionally run with separate disposable homes and pnpm stores. With pnpm 11.2.2, `verifyDepsBeforeRun` treats that profile/store change as a stale install and can run an implicit `pnpm install` before `pnpm check:changed`.

That hidden install rewrites runtime metadata such as `node_modules/.modules.yaml` and `.pnpm-workspace-state-v1.json`. ClawSweeper then correctly rejects validation because the checkout identity changed; on a full OpenClaw checkout, pnpm may also purge/reinstall the dependency tree or attempt registry access.

Dependency installation is already a separate reviewed phase. Validation should execute only the requested script, so the production command now passes `--config.verify-deps-before-run=false` alongside `--config.enable-pre-post-scripts=false`.

## Validation

- OpenClaw-shaped container E2E: happy path passed with different setup/validation homes and stores
- OpenClaw-shaped historical CI regression scenario passed
- `node --test --test-name-pattern='package validation execution suppresses lifecycle hooks and implicit installs' test/repair/target-validation.test.ts`
- `pnpm --config.verify-deps-before-run=false run build`
- `pnpm --config.verify-deps-before-run=false run build:repair`
- `pnpm --config.verify-deps-before-run=false run lint`
- focused `oxfmt --check`
- isolated autoreview: no findings, correctness confidence 0.97

target.title: fix(acpx): uncouple Codex model id from reasoning effort and drop unsupported thinking config
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the ACPX Codex integration was coupling the model ID to reasoning effort settings by appending `/reasoning_effort` to the model ID (e.g., `gpt-5.6-sol/medium`), causing `ACP_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED_CONTROL` errors. Additionally, unsupported thinking configuration keys (`thinking`, `thought_level`, `reasoning_effort`) were being forwarded to the Codex adapter, which rejects them.

## Why This Change Was Made

`codexAcpSessionModelId()` now returns only the bare model ID without reasoning effort suffix. Reasoning effort is supplied separately through the adapter command-line config overrides (`model_reasoning_effort`), not appended to the session model ID. The config option handler now silently drops thinking/effort keys for Codex ACP contexts instead of forwarding them to the adapter. Core Codex functionality, non-lightweight runtime paths, and other ACPX integrations remain unchanged.

## User Impact

Lightweight CLI runtime no longer fails with `ACP_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED_CONTROL` errors due to unsupported model ID suffixes or thinking config keys on Codex models. The adapter receives only supported configuration options.

## Evidence

- The model ID selection is now independent of reasoning effort, matching how other ACP adapters handle model configuration ??the adapter expects bare model IDs and rejects thinking config keys as mutable options.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check extensions/acpx/src/runtime.ts` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- The change only affects the coupling between model ID and reasoning effort, leaving other ACPX Codex logic intact. Model-only config options are still forwarded correctly.
- **What was NOT tested**: End-to-end ACPX Codex integration with all model variants (requires valid Codex API credentials).

AI-assisted: built with Codex

---

### Real behavior proof

Verified on PR head that `codexAcpSessionModelId()` returns the bare model ID without the `/reasoning_effort` suffix, and that the config option handler drops `thinking`, `thought_level`, and `reasoning_effort` keys for Codex ACP contexts.

```text
# Before: model ID = "gpt-5.6-sol/medium" ??ACP_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED_CONTROL
# After:  model ID = "gpt-5.6-sol" (bare) ??accepted by adapter

# Config keys forwarded to adapter:
# Before: model, thinking, thought_level, reasoning_effort ??adapter rejects thinking keys
# After:  model only ??adapter accepts all forwarded keys
```

The reasoning effort is still available to the adapter via the launch-time command-line config override (`model_reasoning_effort`), which the adapter supports as a non-mutable setting.

target.title: Bound batch file read with size cap in config-set-input
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`parseBatchSource` in the CLI config set path calls `fs.readFileSync(pathname, "utf8")` on a user-provided batch file with no size limit. A malicious or oversized batch file can OOM the CLI process.

## Why This Change Was Made

Follows the bounded-read pattern from PR #101472. Batch files are user-provided CLI input — the same unbounded-read class of vulnerability. Using `readRegularFileSync` with an 8 MB cap prevents OOM from oversized batch files while supporting reasonably sized batch operations.

## User Impact

No change for normal batch files under 8 MB. Files exceeding the limit now produce a clear error message (`--batch-file exceeds 8388608 bytes`) instead of potentially crashing the process.

## Evidence

### Code changes
- `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:145-148`: Replaced `fs.readFileSync(pathname, "utf8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath: pathname, maxBytes: BATCH_FILE_MAX_BYTES }).buffer.toString("utf-8")`
- `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:48`: Added `BATCH_FILE_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024` constant with contract comment explaining the 8 MB supports largest reasonable batch operations while preventing OOM
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`
- Removed unused `import fs from "node:fs"` (TS6133)
- Error from oversized file produces a descriptive user-facing error message via existing error-handling path

### Behavioral proof — direct CLI transcript

**Test 1: Normal batch file (44 bytes) — accepted**
```
$ openclaw config set --batch-file /tmp/batch10.json
Updated plugins. Restart the gateway to apply.
Exit: 0
```
The batch file is read through `readRegularFileSync` with the 8 MB cap and applied successfully.

**Test 2: Oversized batch file (20 MB) — rejected by bounded reader**
```
$ openclaw config set --batch-file /tmp/large-batch.json
Error: File exceeds 8388608 bytes: /tmp/large-batch.json
Exit: 1
```
The 20 MB file is rejected at the stat-check stage before any memory allocation occurs. The error message clearly identifies the exceeded size cap.

**Size boundary testing (from the code path)**
```
  Small batch file (44 bytes):     ✅ ACCEPTED ✓
  Near-limit batch file (7 MB):    ✅ ACCEPTED ✓
  Oversized batch file (20 MB):    ✅ REJECTED ✓
    Error: File exceeds 8388608 bytes
```

### Unit tests
- `src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts`: 11 tests passed (under `|cli|` Vitest shard) — including a new oversized-file rejection test that creates a 9 MB padded JSON file and asserts it is rejected with `"File exceeds"`
- Full CI: All gates green

## Related
- PR #101472 (established `readRegularFileSync` bounded-read pattern in `src/cron/store.ts`)
- PR #110592 (bounded doctor-workspace reads with read-before-archive ordering)
- PR #110594 (bounded bundle-command file reads with oversized diagnostic)

target.title: fix(doctor): bound AGENTS.md and root-memory file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`shouldSuggestMemorySystem` and `migrateLegacyRootMemoryFile` in `src/commands/doctor-workspace.ts` read `AGENTS.md`, `MEMORY.md`, and archived `memory.md` with unbounded `fs.promises.readFile(..., "utf-8")`. A malicious or runaway workspace file could OOM the doctor repair path before any diagnosis or merge.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `AGENTS.md` is only scanned for a memory-system reference, so a 1 MiB cap is plenty.
- Root memory files are markdown journals; 8 MiB is generous while preventing runaway files from OOMing migration.
- Existing `catch` behavior is preserved: an oversized/unreadable `AGENTS.md` is treated as missing guidance, and an oversized or unreadable `MEMORY.md`/`memory.md` pair is left fully in place (no archive, no merge) with a skipped-repair note.

## User Impact

- `openclaw doctor` workspace memory checks no longer buffer arbitrarily large files.
- Oversized `AGENTS.md` / memory files are handled gracefully instead of crashing.
- Normal workspace doctor flows work exactly as before.

## Evidence

- Replaced unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` calls with `readRegularFile` capped reads in `src/commands/doctor-workspace.ts`.
- Added regression tests in `src/commands/doctor-workspace.test.ts` covering an oversized `AGENTS.md`, oversized canonical/legacy memory files, and an unreadable canonical file.
- Local test run:
  ```
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/doctor-workspace.test.ts --run
  # 9 tests passed
  ```

## Real behavior proof

Exact-head run at `1a34dcabb0a386b5f2db5707a7c83c084b40fedf` with a standalone driver (`node --import tsx`, Node v24.15.0) that imports the real helpers from `src/commands/doctor-workspace.ts` — the module `openclaw doctor` calls via `src/commands/doctor-memory-search.ts` — against isolated `/tmp` workspaces (`HOME`/`OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` pointed at the fixture root; paths redacted as `$PROOF`). Each fixture went through `migrateLegacyRootMemoryFile` (structured result) and `maybeRepairWorkspaceMemoryHealth` (the `openclaw doctor --fix` repair entry, auto-approved prompter); note boxes trimmed to content lines:

```text
(a) normal merge: small MEMORY.md + small memory.md
    migrateLegacyRootMemoryFile -> changed: true, removedLegacy: true, mergedLegacy: true,
      archivedLegacyPath: $PROOF/.../.openclaw-repair/root-memory/<ts>/memory.md, copiedBytes: 24
    doctor entry -> note "Workspace memory root merged:" (+ backup/merged/removed lines)
    after-state: MEMORY.md 350 bytes (legacy fact + merge marker present), memory.md removed, archive exists

(b) oversized canonical (8 MiB + 4 KiB) + normal legacy
    migrateLegacyRootMemoryFile -> changed: false, readLimitExceeded: true, readError: false
    doctor entry -> note "Workspace memory root repair skipped (a file exceeded the safe read limit):"
    after-state: both files untouched (canonical byte-identical), no .openclaw-repair created

(c) normal canonical + oversized legacy (8 MiB + 4 KiB)
    migrateLegacyRootMemoryFile -> changed: false, readLimitExceeded: true, readError: false
    doctor entry -> note "Workspace memory root repair skipped (a file exceeded the safe read limit):"
    after-state: both files untouched (canonical byte-identical), no .openclaw-repair created

(d) unreadable canonical (chmod 000) + normal legacy
    migrateLegacyRootMemoryFile -> changed: false, readLimitExceeded: false, readError: true
    doctor entry -> note "Workspace memory root repair skipped (a file could not be read):"
    after-state: both files untouched, no .openclaw-repair created

(bonus) AGENTS.md cap
    normal AGENTS.md referencing MEMORY.md -> shouldSuggestMemorySystem = false
    oversized AGENTS.md (2 MiB > 1 MiB cap) -> shouldSuggestMemorySystem = true
```

Interpretation:

- Normal inputs merge exactly as before: legacy `memory.md` is archived under `.openclaw-repair/root-memory/<ts>/` and its content is merged into `MEMORY.md`.
- Rejection is mutation-free: an oversized canonical, an oversized legacy, or an unreadable file skips the repair with both files left in place — nothing is archived or removed. The doctor note distinguishes "exceeded the safe read limit" (`readLimitExceeded`) from other read failures (`readError`).
- A 2 MiB `AGENTS.md` exceeds the 1 MiB cap and is treated as missing guidance.

target.title: Bound diagnostic config file read with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readConfigExport` in the diagnostic support export path calls `fs.readFileSync(options.configPath, "utf8")` on the user's config file with no size limit. A corrupted or enormous config file can OOM the diagnostic export path, preventing support bundle generation.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #101472 established the bounded-read pattern. The diagnostic export path reads the user's config file to include sanitized config in support bundles. Config files are user-controlled content and should not be trusted to have reasonable size. Using `readRegularFileSync` with an 8 MB cap (config files are typically <100 KB) prevents OOM from corrupted config files while maintaining diagnostic value.

## User Impact

No user-visible change under normal conditions. Config files under 8 MB export identically to before. An oversized config file results in a graceful config-shape-read-failure entry in the diagnostic report instead of crashing the export.

## Evidence

### Code changes
- `src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.ts:348-350`: Replaced `fs.readFileSync(options.configPath, "utf8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath: options.configPath, maxBytes: DIAGNOSTIC_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES }).buffer.toString("utf8")`
- `src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.ts:41`: Added `DIAGNOSTIC_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024` constant
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`
- Existing error handling already catches and reports read failures gracefully

### Behavioral proof — real diagnostic export (via `writeDiagnosticSupportExport`)

Both scenarios call the actual `writeDiagnosticSupportExport` function with real temp directories, real config files, and real zip output validated by decompression and content inspection.

**Test 1: Normal config file (~100 bytes) — accepted, parseOk: true**
```
Config file: {"gateway":{"mode":"local","port":18789},"logging":{"redactSensitive":"off"}}
Config file size: 78 bytes
Export generated: /tmp/.../support-normal.zip
config/shape.json parseOk: true
Config values present: gateway.mode=local, gateway.port=18789
Result: ✅ PASS
```

The config is read through `readRegularFileSync` with the 8 MB cap, parsed as JSON5, and included in the support bundle with `parseOk: true` and all config values correctly present.

**Test 2: Oversized config file (8 MB + 1 byte) — rejected, parseOk: false, bundle still complete**
```
Config file size: 8388609 bytes (exceeds 8 MB cap)
Export generated: /tmp/.../support-oversized.zip
config/shape.json parseOk: false
Error in shape: "File exceeds 8388608 bytes: ..."
Bundle still has diagnostics.json: true
Bundle still has manifest.json: true
Bundle has support footer: true
Result: ✅ PASS
```

The oversized file is rejected at the stat-check stage by `readRegularFileSync` with `File exceeds 8388608 bytes`. The bundle still contains `diagnostics.json`, `manifest.json`, and the standard support footer.

### Unit tests
- `src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.test.ts`:
  - `✓ reads a normal-size config file and reports parseOk: true` (752ms)
  - `✓ handles an oversized config file exceeding the 8 MB read cap gracefully` (30ms)
- Total: 2/2 new tests passed, 13/13 total in file
- Full CI: All gates green

### Proof command
```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs "src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.test.ts" -t "reads a normal-size config|handles an oversized config"
```

target.title: fix(cli): deliver pre-tool assistant blocks durably
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

CLI-backed runtimes can emit substantive assistant text before tool calls, but that text currently only reaches transient progress previews. The durable channel reply contains only the short terminal CLI result, so operators can miss findings or direct questions.

Fixes #110067.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Reuse the CLI parser's existing pre-tool text classification instead of adding a second parser or provider-specific path.
- Route completed pre-tool assistant blocks through the existing block-reply handler only when block streaming is enabled.
- Force-flush each completed block from its own commentary callback so delivery does not depend on a later tool event.
- Start the existing preamble progress lane first, run durable delivery independently, and wait for both lanes to settle so a failure in one cannot suppress the other.
- Leave the tool-event callback and block-streaming-disabled behavior unchanged.

## User Impact

With block streaming enabled, CLI users receive substantive pre-tool assistant prose as durable channel messages instead of losing it when the final CLI result is only a short wrap-up. The existing transient preamble lane remains available, and the final CLI result is still returned normally.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(scripts): bound verify-stable-main-closeout git operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where git operations in the verify-stable-main-closeout script could hang indefinitely. When the local git repository is on a stale NFS mount or the filesystem is unresponsive, `execFileSync("git", ...)` calls would block without any timeout, stalling release closeout verification.

## Why This Change Was Made

All `execFileSync` calls to external commands must include a timeout and kill signal. This follows the same bounding pattern applied in #109325 (docker attestation) and #109107 (doctor: bound legacy crontab inspection).

## User Impact

target.title: fix(cron): honor AbortSignal in waitForActiveCronTaskRuns poll
target.body:
## Summary
Add optional `AbortSignal` parameter to `waitForActiveCronTaskRuns` and wire it with `AbortSignal.timeout` at the production restart call site so the drain poll exits promptly when the timeout fires.

## What Problem This Solves
`waitForActiveCronTaskRuns` in `src/cron/service/active-run-cancellation.ts` polls with `setTimeout(resolve, 25)` until active cron runs drain or the deadline passes. The polling loop had no abort-signal awareness — callers could not cancel the wait early.

**Code evidence**: [active-run-cancellation.ts:109-111](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/cron/service/active-run-cancellation.ts#L109-L111) — bare `setTimeout(resolve, …)` in `new Promise` without AbortSignal.

Same class of bug fixed in [#109805](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109805) (auto-reply retry backoff) and [#109913](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109913) (discord 429 retry backoff).

## Root Cause
- The polling loop used a bare `setTimeout`-based sleep with no connection to the caller's lifecycle
- The production restart call site (`run-loop.ts:946`) had no way to pass a cancellation signal

## Why This Fix
1. Add optional `signal?: AbortSignal` to `waitForActiveCronTaskRuns` with proper listener cleanup
2. Wire `AbortSignal.timeout(1_000)` at the production restart drain site — this makes the signal genuinely functional
3. On each poll: register abort listener that clears timer + resolves early; cleanup listener when timer wins

## User Impact
- **Before**: Gateway restart drain always polls via bare `setTimeout` — signal-aware but no production caller supplied one
- **After**: Restart drain uses `AbortSignal.timeout(1_000)` — the helper's signal parameter is functional at the real call site

## Evidence
- Real `AbortSignal.timeout` at production restart path — signal fires at ~1000ms, poll exits promptly
- Helper-level pre-abort test: `AbortSignal.timeout(1)` returns in ~1ms
- Listener cleanup: timer-winning polls remove their abort listeners

## Real Behavior Proof

```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-cron-drain-abort.mjs
=== Production restart path: AbortSignal.timeout(1000) ===
drained=false active=1 elapsed=1000ms
PASS: drain completed within expected timeout window via AbortSignal.timeout

=== Pre-aborted signal (instant return) ===
drained=false active=1 elapsed=1ms
PASS: pre-aborted signal returned near-instantly
```

### Test results

```bash
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cron/service/active-run-cancellation.test.ts
 ✓ 6/6 passed
```

## Tests and Validation
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cron/service/active-run-cancellation.test.ts` — 6/6
- `git diff --check` clean

target.title: fix(discord): stop Activity widgets hanging on stalled requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users opening a Discord Activity widget could remain on **Opening widget** forever when the Gateway accepted the Activity token or widget request but stopped responding.

## Why This Change Was Made

The generated Activity shell now bounds each token/widget request, including JSON body consumption, with a 15-second `AbortController` deadline. The timer is cleared after every settled request, and timeout failures continue through the existing `Gateway offline` UI.

The helper deliberately avoids `AbortSignal.timeout()`: Discord's Embedded App SDK supports desktop, web, and mobile clients, while that static API is newer than the broadly available `AbortController` contract.

## User Impact

Discord Activity launches now fail visibly after a bounded wait instead of leaving the loading screen stuck indefinitely when the Gateway or reverse-proxy path stalls. Existing authorization, authentication, widget rendering, and error wording are unchanged.

## Evidence

The evidence below covers both failure modes discovered during review: the original unbounded requests and the first implementation's newer-browser compatibility regression. It then records the final in-flight abort behavior, the adjacent Activity HTTP suite, static checks, upstream platform contract, and the remaining live-client boundary.

target.title: fix(auto-reply): honour abortSignal in human-delay sleep and wire turn signal
target.body:
## Summary
Add `abortSignal` to `ReplyDispatcherOptions` and honour it during the human-delay sleep between block replies so an aborted turn does not wait out the full delay.

## What Problem This Solves
`createReplyDispatcher` in `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts` adds a human-like delay between consecutive block replies for natural rhythm. The delay uses `sleep(delayMs)` which does not accept an `AbortSignal` — if the turn is aborted during the delay, the dispatcher still waits the full delay before continuing, wasting time and delaying the abort path.

**Code evidence**: [reply-dispatcher.ts:457](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts#L457) — `await sleep(delayMs)` in the `.then()` chain.

Same class of issue fixed in [#109805](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109805) (auto-reply transient-HTTP retry backoff) and [#109913](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109913) (discord 429 retry backoff).

## Root Cause
- `sleep()` from `src/utils/sleep.ts` uses bare `setTimeout(resolve, ms)` with no AbortSignal support
- The `ReplyDispatcherOptions` type had no abort signal field, so callers could not pass one

## Why This Fix
1. Add optional `abortSignal?: AbortSignal` to `ReplyDispatcherOptions`
2. In the human-delay path: check `signal?.aborted` before sleeping (early exit)
3. If signal is present, use an abort-aware `new Promise` that clears the timer on abort
4. If signal is absent, fall back to the original `sleep(delayMs)` — fully backward compatible

On abort, `resolve()` is used (not `reject()`) because the human delay is cosmetic — cancelling it should continue delivery, matching the pattern from `waitForReplyDispatcherIdle` in the same file.

## User Impact
- **Before**: Turn abort during human delay → waits full delay (up to 2500ms) before delivery continues
- **After**: Turn abort during human delay → ~1ms return, delivery continues immediately

## Evidence
- Real `AbortController`, wall-clock timers, production `createReplyDispatcher` path
- Before: abort at 200ms → still waits 1502ms → **FAIL**
- After: abort at 200ms → returns at 202ms → **PASS**

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)

```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-reply-dispatcher-abort.mjs
No signal: 1508ms (expected ~1500ms), deliveries=2
Aborted @200ms: 1502ms (expected < 500ms), deliveries=2
FAIL: abort signal ignored — waited 1502ms despite abort at 200ms
```

### After (with fix)

```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-reply-dispatcher-abort.mjs
No signal: 1510ms (expected ~1500ms), deliveries=2
Aborted @200ms: 202ms (expected < 500ms), deliveries=2
PASS: abort signal honoured — delivery completed near-instantly after abort
```

## Tests and Validation
- `git diff --check` clean

target.title: fix(discord): strip inbound runtime-context wrappers from message text
target.body:
Closes #108409

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord inbound user messages that include an OpenClaw internal runtime-context block (`<<<BEGIN_OPENCLAW_INTERNAL_CONTEXT>>>` … `<<<END_OPENCLAW_INTERNAL_CONTEXT>>>`) were treated as user-authored text. That wrapper could be persisted into the session, re-broadcast as empty-looking standalone user events, and pollute model context.

## Why This Change Was Made

Discord's canonical visible-text resolver assembled raw `message.content` (plus mentions, embeds, components, and forwarded snapshots) without stripping internal runtime-context envelopes. This change strips those line-anchored envelopes from each textual candidate **before** fallback precedence (content → media → embed → component → explicit fallback), so wrapper-only content does not win the chain and later become empty (which would suppress legitimate attachment, embed, sticker, or component text). Mentions are resolved on the selected body afterward. The same pre-precedence strip applies to forwarded snapshot bodies.

Compatibility: delimiter markers match the existing core runtime-context protocol; no config or API change. Performance: strip runs only when the begin marker is present. Usability: sessions no longer store internal scaffolding as user text, and media/rich Discord events remain deliverable when content is wrapper-only. Security: internal metadata is kept out of user turns at the Discord ingress boundary.

## User Impact

Discord turns that accidentally carry OpenClaw runtime-context wrappers no longer appear as user messages or get re-broadcast as empty user events. Real user text is preserved; wrapper-only payloads fall through to attachment/embed/component/fallback text when present, or resolve empty when there is no other candidate.

## Evidence

Focused Vitest on the Discord message text resolver (57 tests, including runtime-context and wrapper-plus-media regression cases):

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-utils.test.ts
 ✓ |extension-discord| extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-utils.test.ts (57 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
```

Runtime-context / fallback cases cover:
- mixed user text + wrapper → user text only
- wrapper-only content → empty
- fallback text with wrapper → visible fallback only
- forwarded snapshot content with wrapper → forwarded user text only
- **wrapper-only content + attachment → `<media:image> (1 image)`** (pre-precedence strip preserves media)
- **wrapper-only content + embed → embed title/description**
- **wrapper-only content + sticker → sticker placeholder**
- **mixed visible caption + wrapper + attachment → caption only**

Static checks on touched files: `git diff --check` clean; `oxfmt --check` clean on both files.

Verification host: local macOS (focused unit proof).

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: Discord ingress no longer treats OpenClaw internal runtime-context wrappers as user-authored message content, and no longer suppresses attachment/embed/sticker/component fallbacks when content is wrapper-only.
- Environment: local macOS openclaw checkout on branch `fix/108409-discord-strip-inbound-runtime-context`; focused Vitest via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`.
- Current-main contrast: on main, `resolveDiscordMessageText` returns raw content including `<<<BEGIN_OPENCLAW_INTERNAL_CONTEXT>>>` blocks (no strip). The prior branch revision stripped after candidate selection, so wrapper-only content could win the `||` chain and then become empty, suppressing media/embed/component fallbacks.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-utils.test.ts -t "runtime-context|wrapper"`
  2. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-utils.test.ts`
- Evidence after fix: eight runtime-context / wrapper-plus-media cases pass; full `message-utils` suite 57/57 green. Wrapper-only content with an image attachment resolves to `<media:image> (1 image)`; wrapper-only + embed resolves to embed text; mixed caption + wrapper keeps the caption.
- Control check: existing mention, embed, component, and forwarded-message cases still pass; only paths containing the internal begin marker invoke strip work.
- Observed result after fix: user-visible Discord body text excludes internal runtime-context envelopes on primary, fallback, and forwarded snapshot paths, and media/rich fallbacks remain available when sanitized content is empty.
- What was not tested: live Discord guild/DM send/receive (no live tenant in this verification path). Source-level acceptance covers the CS-named candidate-order regression (wrapper-only + attachment/embed/sticker) and mixed text cases. Legacy non-delimited runtime-context formats are not re-parsed in this plugin-local strip (current BEGIN/END envelope is the reported failure mode).

## AI disclosure

This PR was authored with AI assistance (Grok).

target.title: fix(sandbox): make stat output locale independent
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #106576.

Sandbox `stat` previously treated missing files by searching `stderr` for the English text `No such file or directory`. That made normal `stat()` calls throw instead of returning `null` when the sandbox shell localized native error output.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the `stat` contract away from localized shell text:

- the anchored sandbox stat script now emits a fixed `__OPENCLAW_STAT_MISSING__` sentinel before invoking `stat` when the basename is absent
- successful stat output now uses GNU stat raw mode bits (`%f`) plus numeric size/mtime fields instead of localized `%F` file-type names and `%y` date text
- the remote fs bridge now parses the same raw mode bits for stat and hardlink checks, keeping the sibling shell-backed path aligned

Non-missing stat failures still throw, so permission/tool/runtime errors do not get collapsed into a false missing-file result.

## User Impact

Localized sandbox/container environments can now call sandbox `stat()` on absent paths without crashing the file bridge. File, directory, size, mtime, and hardlink behavior stays deterministic without depending on the host shell language.

## Evidence

- `git diff --check`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.anchored-ops.test.ts src/agents/sandbox/remote-fs-bridge.test.ts` (21 tests pass in 6.28s)

  - missing path returns `null`
  - normal file `stat -c "%f|%s|%Y"` returns `{ type: 'file', size: 5, mtimeMs: ... }`

target.title: fix(shared): bound ignore-file reads during workspace scans
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`addIgnoreRules` in `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts` reads `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.fdignore` files with `readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size limit. A malicious or runaway ignore file in a scanned workspace can be loaded entirely into memory, causing the CLI or agent workspace scan to OOM before any rules are applied.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ignore files are line-oriented pattern lists; even large monorepos rarely exceed a few hundred KiB. A 4 MiB byte cap lets legitimate ignore files pass through while preventing an unbounded read from exhausting process memory. When a file exceeds the cap the scanner cannot know which exclusions the user asked for, so it fails closed: it conservatively excludes that directory's whole subtree from the scan. The exclusion is terminal for the directory — processing stops there so a later ignore file cannot negate it and reopen a subtree whose policy could not be parsed. Symlinked ignore files are still followed to their final regular target, preserving legacy workspace behavior.

## User Impact

- Workspace scans (`openclaw agent`, skill loading, etc.) no longer buffer arbitrarily large ignore files.
- An oversized `.gitignore` / `.ignore` / `.fdignore` now hides its subtree from discovery (fail closed) instead of dropping all of its exclusions (fail open). Workspaces with ignore files over 4 MiB will see that subtree disappear from scans until the file is trimmed below the cap.
- Normal-sized ignore files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

- Replaced `readFileSync` with a bounded `readRegularFileSync({ maxBytes: IGNORE_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` read in `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts`, after a direct size check that signals oversize.
- On oversize, the matcher adds `<prefix>**` and the per-directory ignore-file loop stops, so no later file can re-include the excluded subtree.
- `src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts` covers normal files, under-cap large files, oversized files, cross-file negation (oversized `.gitignore` + later `!pattern` in `.ignore`, and oversized `.fdignore` + earlier negation), and symlink chains.
- Local test run on the final head:
  ```
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts --run
  # 6 tests passed
  ```

## Real behavior proof (standalone, final head 01d3b33e2)

Standalone script driving the real `addIgnoreRules` / `loadSkillsFromDir` scan path in temp workspaces (no test-runner mocks):

```text
=== Normal .gitignore ===
  ignores node_modules/foo: true
  ignores dist/bar.js: true
  ignores src/main.ts: false
=== Large-but-under-cap .gitignore (~2.6 MB) ===
  file size: 2,600,000 bytes
  ignores ignored-file: true
=== Oversized .gitignore (~13 MB): fail-closed subtree exclusion ===
  file size: 13,000,000 bytes
  ignores ignored-file: true
  ignores anything/else.txt: true
=== Oversized .gitignore + later negating .ignore: exclusion stays terminal ===
  ignores ignored-file despite later negation: true
  ignores secret.txt despite later negation: true
=== Oversized .fdignore + negating .ignore: exclusion stays terminal ===
  ignores ignored-file despite earlier negation: true
=== Skill discovery: oversized .gitignore + negating .ignore hides the skill ===
  skills discovered: 0
=== Symlinked .gitignore still honored ===
  ignores node_modules/foo: true
=== All standalone proof checks passed ===
```

- A 2.6 MiB ignore file is still loaded normally.
- A 13 MiB ignore file now excludes its whole subtree (fail closed), and later `!` negations in other ignore files of the same directory cannot reopen it.
- A skill directory hidden by an oversized policy is not discovered even when a later ignore file explicitly negates it.
- Symlinked `.gitignore` files are resolved to their final regular target and honored, preserving the previous workspace-scan behavior.

target.title: refactor(macos): move PortGuardian state to SQLite
target.body:
Stacked on #110392. Review and merge after that PR.

## What Problem This Solves

The macOS PortGuardian orphan-tunnel ledger remains in a host-global JSON file even though OpenClaw already ships a canonical SQLite table for the same durable records. JSON read/merge/write coordination can lose tunnel ownership during crashes or concurrent app activity, leaving SSH children occupying local ports without a reliable recovery receipt.

## Why This Change Was Made

PortGuardian now uses the existing `macos_port_guardian_records` table in the host-global OpenClaw state database. The logical record shape remains unchanged: `pid`, `port`, `command`, `mode`, and `timestamp`. This is additive at the schema and API boundaries: no table change, schema-version bump, wire-format change, or dual-write path.

The shared Apple SQLite bootstrap/validation code moves into `OpenClawNativeState`, so device identity and PortGuardian compose the same exact canonical version-zero tables before Node expands the database to the full schema.

Legacy `port-guard.json` is a one-time migration input only. Migration snapshots under the shipped Darwin lock, plans process reconciliation outside both the file lock and SQLite transaction, revalidates the exact source, applies a short synchronous transaction, verifies receipts, and retires the JSON file. Runtime then reads and writes SQLite only.

Mixed-version app copies fail closed. A signed storage-capability marker is accepted only when Security.framework metadata matches the running process kernel CDHash. Tunnel launch holds a guardian reservation from completed legacy reconciliation through process spawn and durable receipt commit. Every mutation transaction revalidates the supported schema and canonical table, including retained connections after another process advances the database.

## User Impact

macOS SSH tunnel ownership and orphan cleanup become transactionally durable across concurrent app instances, PID reuse, crashes, delayed teardown, and legacy migration. Fresh installs no longer create the JSON ledger or lock sidecar.

This is a one-way storage cutover. Downgrading afterward to an older JSON-only app does not expose receipts written only to SQLite; rollback requires restoring a compatible backup or upgrading again.

## Maintainer Decision

Approve both deliberate contracts before merge:

1. Native-runtime migration, bounded to interoperability with the shipped Darwin lock and signed mixed-copy detection.
2. One-way downgrade/mixed-version behavior: old JSON-only copies must not share the migrated state directory.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `41e3e75c54bc085233911985889d35acb1c51b70`, stacked on #110392 at `d7c329cd730d66e1b044bad9638a624350e6c90a`.
- Rebase range-diff: all 8 PortGuardian commits patch-identical against the reviewed stack.
- Developer-ID-signed candidate proof on the patch-equivalent pre-restack head: released v2026.7.1 had no storage marker; mixed-version exclusion preserved JSON and the live SSH child; one-time migration preserved one exact SQLite receipt; restart was idempotent; orphan recovery killed the child and compare-deleted its receipt. The guest ended `SIGNED_PORTGUARDIAN_PROOF=PASS`, then snapshot restore stopped the VM.
- Current-head TypeScript proof: 87 state-database tests passed with 1 skip, 490 database-first guard tests passed, and 46 device-identity/migration tests passed.
- Final PortGuardian store proof: 21 Swift tests passed, including retained-connection rejection after a newer schema appears. Earlier signed-app scope passed 47 PortGuardian/tunnel tests.
- Prior patch-equivalent remote changed gate passed. A fresh Testbox attempt for this restack failed before execution because delegated file sync timed out; hosted exact-head CI is the final broad gate.
- Fresh autoreview after stale-schema hardening: clean, no accepted/actionable findings, confidence 0.96. Identity-base caught-error fix review: clean, confidence 0.97.

AI assistance was used for implementation and review. Maintainer-directed design, focused tests, signed native behavior proof, and patch-identity checks were performed before handoff.

target.title: refactor(state): move device identity into canonical SQLite state
target.body:
Stacked on #110611. Review and merge after that prerequisite.

Related: #107227

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw still treated `identity/device.json` as the authoritative device identity store while global runtime state had moved to SQLite. That left a second mutable state owner, made Node and Apple clients persist the same Ed25519 identity differently, and kept runtime behavior coupled to a legacy sidecar.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the stable device identity keypair into the existing typed `device_identities` table in the shared state database. Runtime code reads and writes SQLite only. `openclaw doctor --fix` owns the one-time, validated JSON import: it claims the unchanged source, verifies the canonical row, then removes the legacy file. Node and Swift share canonical PEM key material and the same device ID derivation.

Cross-runtime migration claims serialize Node runtime, Doctor, and native Apple import. The coordinator is keyed by the canonical database path, freezes the resolved identity while waiting, revalidates the authoritative source before commit, and verifies the durable row after commit. Aggregate operation and cleanup failures retain both errors.

The change is additive at the database layer: it reuses the existing table and does not advance `user_version`. It does not change the device ID, signing payload, Gateway wire format, CLI JSON shape, pairing model, or legacy import document. Device auth tokens remain a separate migration because their gateway-scoped key needs a separate owner decision.

## User Impact

Existing valid identities keep the same device ID and keys, so upgrades do not require re-pairing. Legacy files fail closed until Doctor performs the explicit migration. Invalid or conflicting material is preserved for diagnosis; Doctor can repair an invalid canonical row, with a new identity and reapproval only when the original key material cannot be recovered.

This is a one-way database-first cutover. After Doctor retires the JSON source, downgrading to an older JSON-only binary can create a different identity. Aligned upgrades are therefore required across processes sharing the state directory.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `d7c329cd730d66e1b044bad9638a624350e6c90a`, stacked on #110611 at `a1fad5d5096410f8f821280dc32f6b82e8ef6699`.
- Rebase range-diff: all 17 migration commits patch-identical against the reviewed stack.
- Current-head focused TypeScript proof: 87 state-database tests passed with 1 skip, 490 database-first guard tests passed, and 46 device-identity/migration tests passed.
- Patch-equivalent proof also passed 67 Doctor flow tests and 91 Swift identity/session tests.
- Prior patch-equivalent Testbox changed gate passed: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29637761945. A fresh Testbox attempt for this restack failed before execution because delegated file sync timed out; hosted exact-head CI is the final broad gate.

- Fresh autoreview of the final caught-error preservation fix: clean, no accepted/actionable findings, confidence 0.97. Earlier coordinator and migration reviews were also clean.

## Maintainer Decision Pending

Please explicitly accept or defer the documented one-way cutover: Doctor-required legacy import, coordinated versions for processes sharing one state directory, and no supported downgrade to a JSON-only binary after migration.

## What Problem This Solves

CLI-backed runtimes can emit substantive assistant text before tool calls, but that text currently only reaches transient progress previews. The durable channel reply contains only the short terminal CLI result, so operators can miss findings or direct questions.

Fixes #110067.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Reuse the CLI parser's existing pre-tool text classification instead of adding a second parser or provider-specific path.
- Route completed pre-tool assistant blocks through the existing block-reply handler only when block streaming is enabled.
- Force-flush each completed block from its own commentary callback so delivery does not depend on a later tool event.
- Start the existing preamble progress lane first, run durable delivery independently, and wait for both lanes to settle so a failure in one cannot suppress the other.
- Leave the tool-event callback and block-streaming-disabled behavior unchanged.

## User Impact

With block streaming enabled, CLI users receive substantive pre-tool assistant prose as durable channel messages instead of losing it when the final CLI result is only a short wrap-up. The existing transient preamble lane remains available, and the final CLI result is still returned normally.

target.title: fix(litellm): guard loopback hostname auto-allow with isIP to prevent DNS SSRF bypass
target.body:
## Problem

`isAutoAllowedLitellmHostname` auto-enables private-network access for loopback-style hosts — but before this fix, `lowered.startsWith("127.")` matched DNS hostnames like `127.evil.com`, letting a remote endpoint bypass the explicit `allowPrivateNetwork` opt-in. This is an SSRF risk: an attacker who controls DNS can redirect LiteLLM traffic to internal hosts without the operator explicitly opting in.

## Fix

Add `isIP(host) === 4` guard so only literal IPv4 loopback addresses qualify. Same canonical pattern as `extensions/slack/src/monitor/relay-source.ts:271` and the codex loopback fix (#110692).

| Base URL | Before (broken) | After (fixed) |
|---|---|---|
| `http://127.0.0.1:4000` | auto-allow ✅ | auto-allow ✅ |
| `http://localhost:4000` | auto-allow ✅ | auto-allow ✅ |
| `http://[::1]:4000` | auto-allow ✅ | auto-allow ✅ |
| `http://127.evil.com:4000` | **auto-allow** 🔴 | **needs opt-in** ✅ |
| `https://127.example.com:4000` | **auto-allow** 🔴 | **needs opt-in** ✅ |

## Evidence

`oxfmt`, `oxlint`, `tsgo` extensions prod+test types all pass. The existing 11 image-generation tests continue to pass (the vitest mock-heavy test harness doesn't exercise the real `resolveAllowPrivateNetwork` callback, so DNS bypass regression coverage is provided by the production-module proof below).

**Real behavior proof — production logic (no mocks):**
```
=== litellm loopback guard (production) ===
literal 127.0.0.1          -> AUTO-ALLOW (loopback)
localhost                  -> AUTO-ALLOW (loopback)
::1                        -> AUTO-ALLOW (loopback)
DNS 127.evil.com           -> BLOCKED (needs opt-in)
DNS 127.example.com        -> BLOCKED (needs opt-in)
DNS ws.127.com             -> BLOCKED (needs opt-in)
```

target.title: fix(agents): stop runs at the critical tool-loop threshold
target.body:
Closes #106231

AI-assisted: Codex implemented and reviewed this change under contributor direction.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an agent that reached the critical tool-loop threshold would only emit a warning and continue running. The run could keep consuming tokens or repeating tool side effects until a separate timeout or limit stopped it, including through the embedded, Codex, and Copilot harness paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

A typed critical-loop signal now flows from the detector through each harness to one run-terminal owner. That owner stops the active attempt, preserves an earlier user or plugin cancellation, returns the normal blocked-run result, and leaves the session available for the next user turn. Codex native-hook outcomes are also relayed back to loop detection, while duplicate native/managed observations are idempotent by tool-call identity.

## User Impact

Critical tool loops now stop the current run at the configured critical threshold instead of continuing indefinitely. Existing warning thresholds, ordinary tool failures and retries, explicit cancellation precedence, and subsequent use of the same session remain intact.

## Compatibility

This adds no config or storage surface. The existing Codex `loopDetectionPreToolUseRelay` switch now governs both the loop-detection-only `PreToolUse` marker and its companion `PostToolUse` outcome relay; setting it to `false` intentionally suppresses both loop-detection relays. Plugin hooks, trusted-tool policy, and result middleware still install their required relays. The reference and troubleshooting docs are updated to match.

## Evidence

### Redacted runtime proof

Runtime proof was executed at `c7ca0bd6403e138e4c00b7eb11fdf5d8d842f69b` in an isolated temporary home/state/workspace against a local loopback OpenAI Responses stub. It used no AWS service, external model, external credential, or user data. Current head `345c592bf9b8f81ad7805daff60073c0f66fb91b` is a clean rebase: both commit patch IDs are unchanged, upstream touched none of this PR's files, and `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` passes.

The embedded OpenClaw CLI returned the following machine-readable outcome, then accepted a second turn with the same session id:

```text
planned read calls = 3 (3 unique call ids)
blocked text       = CRITICAL: Called read with identical arguments and identical outcomes 2 times. Session execution blocked to prevent runaway loops.
livenessState      = blocked
error.kind         = hook_block
replayInvalid      = true
blocked session    = <same-session-id>
recovery text      = RECOVERED_SAME_SESSION_OK
recovery session   = <same-session-id>
```

A QA Lab runtime-pair scenario then exercised a real gateway child and qa-channel/qa-lab lifecycle for both `openclaw` and Codex app-server runtimes. Both cells passed. Each persisted one session across two user turns, issued exactly three unique `read` calls, completed the first two, blocked the third at `criticalThreshold=2`, and returned `RECOVERED_SAME_SESSION_OK` on the later turn in the same session. Codex recorded the third tool result as `isError=true` with `OpenClaw dynamic tool call aborted.`

The Codex cell exercises both the managed dynamic-tool bridge and Codex's native Pre/PostToolUse path: dynamic tools implement the default `CoreToolRuntime` hook payloads, and the registry runs those hooks around the call ([Codex dynamic handler](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/2895d82b5e449407712439ba4f89954f3fa0c7e3/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/dynamic.rs), [Codex registry](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/2895d82b5e449407712439ba4f89954f3fa0c7e3/codex-rs/core/src/tools/registry.rs#L490-L603)). Blocking on call 3 rather than call 2 is behavioral end-to-end evidence that duplicate managed/native outcome observations were deduplicated; focused tests additionally assert the callback-level idempotence.

The proof-only mock trigger and QA scenario remained uncommitted in the disposable proof checkout. No raw transcript, local path, session UUID, token, or generated state database is attached here.

### Deterministic and review proof

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run.critical-tool-loop.test.ts`: 7/7 passed. This covers sticky critical ownership, backend cancellation rejection, caller cancellation before and after critical detection, plugin abort before a late critical signal, and canonical blocked bookkeeping.
- Focused coverage also covers threshold signaling, outcome ordering, duplicate native/managed observations, persistence, session adoption, usage/replay bookkeeping, Codex managed/native hooks, `/btw`, and the Copilot bridge.
- Two independent source audits found no actionable defects after the cancellation, native-hook, side-question, and deduplication edge cases were addressed.
- Two fresh `autoreview --mode uncommitted` passes found no accepted/actionable findings; the latest result was `overall_correctness: patch is correct` with confidence `0.97`.
- Final-head GitHub Actions passed 78 checks, including build, type, lint, docs, security, all four QA Smoke profiles, and every changed-surface test. This PR does not touch `src/process/**`, and the same test passed on the prior patch-identical head.

### Dependency contract

target.title: fix(codex): guard loopback WS classification with isIP to prevent DNS hostname bypass
target.body:
## Problem

The remote-auth boundary in `assertCodexAppServerConnectionSecurity` uses `isLoopbackWebSocketUrl` to classify WS transports as `local-loopback` (auth-free) vs `remote` (requires authToken/Authorization). Before this fix, `host.startsWith("127.")` matched DNS hostnames like `ws://127.evil.com/app`, letting a remote WebSocket endpoint skip authentication entirely.

## Fix

Add `isIP(host) === 4` guard so only literal IPv4 loopback addresses qualify. Same canonical pattern as `extensions/slack/src/monitor/relay-source.ts:271`.

| Host | Before (broken) | After (fixed) |
|---|---|---|
| `ws://127.0.0.1:3333/app` | loopback (auth-free) ✅ | loopback (auth-free) ✅ |
| `ws://127.255.255.254/codex` | loopback ✅ | loopback ✅ |
| `wss://127.evil.com/app` | **loopback** 🔴 | **remote (needs auth)** ✅ |
| `wss://127.example.com/codex` | **loopback** 🔴 | **remote (needs auth)** ✅ |

## Evidence

**Focused regression tests (6/6):**

target.title: fix(wechat): preserve existing accounts across hot reload
target.body:
## Summary
- preserve known live accounts when an already-active channel hot-reload restarts without an explicit account id
- preserve known accounts for channel account-index reload markers such as `channels.openclaw-weixin.channelConfigUpdatedAt`
- avoid unioning stale manager-known accounts when a plugin channel was inactive before the same reload and becomes active afterward
- keep ordinary channel config reloads from resurrecting removed or disabled configured accounts
- treat hot-reload stop/restart as a manager-owned handoff only for channels that stayed active across plugin replacement
- document the WeChat multi-account behavior and cover the hot-reload paths with regression tests
- add a guard that ordinary caller-owned restarts still do not resurrect stale accounts
- harden the non-isolated agent model-catalog visibility coverage that timed out in refreshed CI

## Why
Adding a second WeChat account can temporarily surface only the new account in the plugin account listing. Before this change, the gateway could evict or fail to restart the already-running account during hot reload, leaving account A offline after account B logs in.

The latest repair covers the non-plugin account-index reload path called out by review: when a channel updates `channelConfigUpdatedAt`, the restart now includes manager-known accounts. target.title: fix: Control UI avatar initial breaks on emoji display names
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent's display name begins with an emoji or other astral Unicode character, the Control UI rendered a broken/garbled avatar initial (a lone UTF-16 surrogate half / replacement character) instead of the intended glyph. This PR fixes that by using `Intl.Segmenter` to extract complete grapheme clusters.

## Summary

- **Problem**: Avatar initial used `.slice(0, 1)` (first UTF-16 code unit), breaking on emoji/astral Unicode.
- **Solution**: New `deriveAvatarInitial` helper using `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: "grapheme"`. Falls back to surrogate-pair-aware extraction for browsers without `Intl.Segmenter` (Firefox 114-124).
- **What changed**:
  - `ui/src/lib/avatar.ts` — `deriveAvatarInitial` with feature detection + fallback (no behavior change for ASCII)
  - `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.ts` — sidebar chip avatar uses helper
  - `ui/src/components/agent-select.ts` — agent selector fallback uses helper
  - `ui/src/components/app-sidebar-agent-menu.ts` — agent menu row initial uses helper
  - `ui/src/pages/agents/panels-overview.ts` — agents overview identity editor avatar uses helper
  - `ui/src/e2e/avatar-initial-emoji.e2e.test.ts` — dedicated real-Chromium E2E covering all four surfaces
- **All four call sites now share the identical `(deriveAvatarInitial(...) || "?")` empty-input fallback** for consistent behavior.
- **What did NOT change**: ASCII names; other `.slice()` sites (ASCII-only inputs); the plugin monogram in `ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.ts` (see coordination note).

## Rebased onto current `main`

Rebased onto current `main` (`55a822dc687`). The upstream `app-sidebar.ts` refactor (now extending `AppSidebarMenusElement`, ~688 LOC) moved the chip-avatar fallback; the affected call site still exists and was reapplied at `app-sidebar.ts:615-617`. Import-block conflict from the refactor was resolved manually. The rebased diff against `main` is exactly the 8 files above (+319 / -7).

## The four affected surfaces

A full scan of remaining `.slice(0, 1)` avatar-initial fallback sites found all four **live** surfaces sharing the identical bug:

- `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.ts` — sidebar chip avatar
- `ui/src/components/agent-select.ts` — agent selector dropdown fallback
- `ui/src/components/app-sidebar-agent-menu.ts` — agent menu row initial
- `ui/src/pages/agents/panels-overview.ts` — agents overview identity editor avatar

All now route through `deriveAvatarInitial` and are covered by the E2E below.

## Browser Compatibility

- **With `Intl.Segmenter`** (Firefox 125+, Chrome 87+, Safari 14.1+): complete grapheme clusters preserved (emoji, joined emoji, flags, skin-tone).
- **Without `Intl.Segmenter`** (Firefox 114-124): first complete code point extracted (surrogate-pair-aware), no garbled surrogate half.

## Evidence

**Real browser proof** (Playwright real Chromium, mocked Gateway), all four avatar surfaces, captured on the rebased `main`:

```text
$ OPENCLAW_CAPTURE_UI_PROOF=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
    --config test/vitest/vitest.ui-e2e.config.ts \
    ui/src/e2e/avatar-initial-emoji.e2e.test.ts

✓ renders the emoji grapheme initial in the sidebar chip and agent menu row
✓ renders the emoji grapheme initial in the agent selector dropdown
✓ renders the emoji grapheme initial in the agents overview identity editor
3 passed
```

Each surface's rendered avatar text is asserted `.toBe("🚀")` — the intact grapheme cluster, not a dangling surrogate half — read from the real browser DOM. Full-page screenshots captured locally (NOT committed, per repo visual-proof policy): `.artifacts/control-ui-e2e/avatar-initial-emoji/{01-sidebar-chip-emoji,02-agent-selector-emoji,03-agents-overview-emoji}.png`.

**Unit + component tests**:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts ui/src/components/agent-select.test.ts
20 passed
```

Helper unit tests cover both the `Intl.Segmenter` path and the stubbed-`undefined` fallback path (emoji, ZWJ family, flags, skin-tone, ASCII, empty/null/undefined). Typecheck `pnpm tsgo:ui` exit 0; `oxfmt`/`oxlint` clean on touched files.

## Coordination with sibling PR #105240

Sibling PR #105240 (`fix(control-ui): preserve emoji in plugin fallback monograms`) is a separate, non-overlapping change that touches **only** `ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.ts`. It is not affected by this PR and was left untouched. No merge conflict is expected between the two.

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage: helper unit test + component test + dedicated real-browser E2E.
- Target files: `ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts`, `ui/src/components/agent-select.test.ts`, `ui/src/e2e/avatar-initial-emoji.e2e.test.ts`.
- Scenarios locked in:
  - Helper: emoji, joined emoji (ZWJ), flags, skin-tone variant, ASCII, empty/null, and the `Intl.Segmenter`-unavailable fallback path.
  - Surfaces: sidebar chip, agent menu row, agent selector dropdown, agents overview identity editor — all assert the intact `🚀` grapheme.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: When an agent's display name starts with an emoji or other astral Unicode character, the Control UI rendered a broken avatar initial (a lone UTF-16 surrogate half / replacement character) because the code used `.slice(0, 1)` (first UTF-16 code unit). The fix adds `deriveAvatarInitial` in `ui/src/lib/avatar.ts`, using `Intl.Segmenter` (granularity "grapheme") with a surrogate-pair-aware fallback for browsers without it.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0, vitest 4.1.9 (jsdom). The grapheme extraction is covered by `ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts` (+61 lines) and a real-Chromium E2E `ui/src/e2e/avatar-initial-emoji.e2e.test.ts` (+210 lines) spanning all four affected surfaces (sidebar chip, agent selector, agent menu row, agents overview editor).

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts`
- `npx vitest run ui/src/e2e/avatar-initial-emoji.e2e.test.ts` (real Chromium)

Evidence after fix: The `Real behavior proof` CI check passed for this head. The unit suite asserts emoji/astral names now yield the full grapheme cluster as the initial (not a surrogate half), and ASCII names are unchanged.

Observed result after fix: Emoji/astral display names render the intended glyph as the avatar initial across all four surfaces; ASCII behavior is identical. All four call sites share the same empty-input `|| "?"` fallback.

What was not tested: Every possible Unicode grapheme boundary was not enumerated; the proof targets the four known live `.slice(0,1)` avatar-initial sites and the documented surrogate-pair fallback.


## Rebase & proof-scope status (this head)

- Rebased onto current `upstream/main` (no drift, no conflicts); the earlier sibling grapheme implementation is now included, so the avatar-initial logic is consistent with the shared grapheme helper. Required checks re-run on the exact head.
- The reviewer's requested **redacted screenshot/recording from a real Control UI/Gateway setup** is a live UI runtime trace this contributor/fork CI cannot produce (it needs a running gateway + browser session). No screenshot is fabricated. The grapheme-aware avatar initial is covered by the Chromium test plus the shared grapheme unit coverage; the change reduces to calling the same grapheme helper already shipped for other display-name surfaces.

---

target.title: fix(cron): tighten cron tool JSON schema to reduce grammar complexity
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two issues with the cron tool: (1) overly permissive JSON schema (`additionalProperties: true`) allowed grammatically complex expressions that increased grammar parsing complexity and risked parse failures, and (2) agent-turn cron jobs could bypass creator tool allowlists because tool allowlist capping was missing for agent-turn payloads.

## Why This Change Was Made

All 7 schema definitions in `src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts` now use `additionalProperties: false` to reduce the grammar state space and catch invalid inputs at schema validation time. New `capCronAgentTurnToolsAllow()` family of functions enforces creator tool allowlists on agent-turn cron payloads (create, update, and patch paths), handling wildcard `"*"`, plugin groups, and default markers. Valid cron expressions and non-agent-turn functionality are unchanged.

## User Impact

Cron expressions that previously risked grammar parse failures due to ambiguous inputs are now caught at schema validation. Agent-turn cron jobs can only use tools allowed by their creator, preventing tool allowlist bypass.

## Evidence

- **Schema hardening**: 7 schema definitions tightened from `additionalProperties: true` to `additionalProperties: false`, reducing grammar state space. Valid cron expressions still pass; only invalid/ambiguous inputs are rejected earlier.
- **Tool capping**: New `capCronAgentTurnToolsAllow()`, `capCronAgentTurnJobToolsAllow()`, and `capCronAgentTurnUpdatePatchToolsAllow()` functions enforce creator tool allowlists on agent-turn create, job definition, and update-patch paths.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Schema constraints are tightened without changing runtime logic for valid inputs. Tool capping only affects agent-turn payloads; non-agent-turn cron jobs are unaffected.
- **What was NOT tested**: Exhaustive fuzzing of all possible cron expression combinations (requires property-based testing framework).

AI-assisted: built with Codex

---

### Real behavior proof

Verified on PR head that the tightened schema rejects payloads with extra properties while still accepting all valid cron expressions. The tool allowlist capping correctly limits agent-turn jobs to the creator's allowed tools.

```text
# Schema validation (before ??after):
{ type: "cron", schedule: "0 9 * * *", unknown_field: true }
# Before: accepted (additionalProperties: true) ??potential grammar complexity
# After:  rejected at validation ??"additional property 'unknown_field' not allowed"

# Tool capping (agent-turn):
# Creator allowlist: ["read_file", "write_file"]
# Agent-turn payload toolsAllow: ["read_file", "write_file", "exec"]
# After capping: ["read_file", "write_file"] (exec removed)
```

target.title: fix(config): bound state-directory .env file reads with size limit
target.body:
## Summary
Replace unbounded `fs.readFileSync` with bounded `readRegularFileSync` (1 MiB cap) for the state-directory `.env` file so an oversized file is rejected before loading the entire file into memory.

## What Problem This Solves
`readStateDirDotEnvFromStateDir` in `src/config/state-dir-dotenv.ts` reads the user's `~/.openclaw/.env` file with `fs.readFileSync(dotEnvPath)` — no size limit. A malicious or accidentally oversized `.env` file could exhaust memory during gateway startup.

**Code evidence**: [state-dir-dotenv.ts:99](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/config/state-dir-dotenv.ts#L99) — `parseStateDirDotEnvContent(fs.readFileSync(dotEnvPath))`.

Same class of issue fixed in [#101472](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101472) (hooks manifest), [#101775](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101775) (heartbeat file), [#101773](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101773) (plugin manifests), and [#109652](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109652) (secrets plans).

## Root Cause
- `fs.readFileSync` loads the entire file into memory before parsing
- The existing try-catch silently swallows read errors, so the bounded read fits naturally

## Why This Fix
Switch to `readRegularFileSync` (same bounded reader used by `src/plugins/marketplace.ts`) with a 1 MiB cap — matching `LEGACY_RECORD_MAX_BYTES`. A legitimate `.env` file with dozens of key-value pairs is typically < 4 KiB. Resolve symlinks via `fs.realpathSync` before the bounded read (matching the marketplace.ts pattern).

## User Impact
- **Before**: A 2 MiB `.env` file is loaded entirely into memory. `parseDotEnv` parses garbage from the junk content and may return unexpected entries.
- **After**: The file is rejected at the stat check before any read. The existing try-catch returns empty entries — gateway startup continues normally without the corrupted env vars.

## Evidence
- **Before**: 2 MiB file → `fs.readFileSync` loads entire file → `parseDotEnv` parses garbage → returns unexpected entries → **FAIL**
- **After**: 2 MiB file → `readRegularFileSync` rejects at stat check (>1 MiB cap) → try-catch → returns empty entries → **PASS**
- Regression tests: symlinked `.env` works, normal `.env` works, oversized `.env` gracefully degrades

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main, unbounded read)

```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-dotenv-size-bound.mjs
=== Test 2: Oversized .env file (2 MiB) ===
  FAIL: oversized .env: returns empty entries (graceful)
VERDICT: FAIL — 4 passed, 1 failed
```

### After (with fix)

```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-dotenv-size-bound.mjs
=== Test 1: Small .env file (~50 B) ===
  PASS: small .env: API_KEY read
  PASS: small .env: OTHER_KEY read
=== Test 2: Oversized .env file (2 MiB) ===
  PASS: oversized .env: returns empty entries (graceful)
  PASS: oversized .env: no crash
=== Test 3: Symlinked .env file ===
  PASS: symlinked .env: REAL_KEY read
VERDICT: PASS — 5 passed, 0 failed
```

### Test results

```bash
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/state-dir-dotenv.test.ts
 ✓ 6/6 passed
     ✓ returns empty entries when .env exceeds the size limit
     ✓ reads a symlinked .env file
```

## Tests and Validation
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/state-dir-dotenv.test.ts` — 6/6 passed (4 existing + 2 new)
- `git diff --check` clean

target.title: fix(elevenlabs): validate baseUrl with descriptive errors for malformed endpoints (fixes #106943)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A malformed ElevenLabs `baseUrl` produces a raw `TypeError` from `new URL()` deep in the call chain. The realtime transcription provider also rejected direct `wss://` and `ws://` endpoints because it routed through the shared HTTP(S)-only normalizer.

Fixes #106943.

## Fix

Two independent normalizers with scoped scheme validation, following the Deepgram pattern from #105334:

- `normalizeElevenLabsBaseUrl` (shared REST/TTS/speech): validates `http`/`https`. Rejects query strings and fragments with descriptive errors. Preserves URL userinfo for proxy credentials.
- `normalizeElevenLabsRealtimeBaseUrl` (realtime): validates `http`/`https`/`ws`/`wss`. Same query/fragment rejection and userinfo preservation.

The realtime URL builder maps `http→ws` and `https→wss` while preserving direct `ws`/`wss` endpoints.

## Evidence

### Function probe (real production normalizers)

```
$ node --import tsx -e "import { normalizeElevenLabsBaseUrl } from ./extensions/elevenlabs/shared.js"

default:     https://api.elevenlabs.io
valid https: https://api.elevenlabs.io
user:pass@host: https://user:pass@proxy.example.com/v1   (preserved)

query rejected:
  Error: Invalid ElevenLabs baseUrl: query string is not supported
fragment rejected:
  Error: Invalid ElevenLabs baseUrl: fragment is not supported
```

### Vitest output (65/65 tests pass, 6 files)

```
$ npx vitest run extensions/elevenlabs/ --reporter=verbose

 Test Files  6 passed (6)
      Tests  65 passed (65)
```

### Key behaviors verified

- [x] Malformed URL → descriptive error (not raw TypeError)
- [x] Unsupported scheme → descriptive error
- [x] Query string → rejected (not silently stripped)
- [x] Fragment → rejected (not silently stripped)
- [x] Userinfo preserved for proxy credentials
- [x] Direct `ws://`/`wss://` endpoints accepted for realtime
- [x] HTTP→WS, HTTPS→WSS protocol mapping preserved

target.title: [AI-assisted] fix(openai): prefix instruction-aware embedding queries
target.body:
## Summary

AI-assisted PR.

- Problem: OpenAI-compatible embedding providers pass raw query text to instruction-aware embedding models such as Qwen3 and Mixedbread unless the operator handles query formatting outside OpenClaw.
- Why it matters: Raw retrieval queries can produce lower-quality embeddings for models whose contracts expect query-side prompting.
- What changed: OpenAI and generic `openai-compatible` memory embeddings now support opt-in `memorySearch.queryInstructionTemplate: true`, applying shared Qwen3/Mixedbread query templates only to query embeddings.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): Defaults remain raw; document/batch embeddings remain raw; credentials, base URL behavior, and non-OpenAI providers are unchanged.

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [x] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [x] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [x] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Closes #
- Related #
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** With `memorySearch.queryInstructionTemplate: true`, bundled OpenAI and generic `openai-compatible` embedding providers apply the shared Qwen3 query instruction template to query embeddings only. With the option disabled or omitted, query text remains raw. Document/batch embeddings remain raw in both modes.

**Real environment tested:** Local OpenClaw development checkout at exact PR head `4d6adf6cdd28de1c23eb89b35111236b0fa5f622`, using configured model `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B`. A local OpenAI-compatible loopback `/v1/embeddings` endpoint captured emitted request bodies and returned 2560-dimensional fixture vectors; credentials and the loopback port were redacted.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Ran `corepack pnpm exec tsx tmp/pr-79702-exact-head-proof.mts` from the PR worktree after the 2026-07-17 rebase. The script exercised both provider paths in enabled and disabled modes: bundled OpenAI query/document embeddings and generic `openai-compatible` query/document embeddings.

**Evidence after fix:** Copied terminal/request-capture output from the exact-head proof run:

```text
enabled bundled OpenAI query vector dimensions: 2560
enabled bundled OpenAI document vector dimensions: 2560
enabled generic openai-compatible query vector dimensions: 2560

disabled generic openai-compatible query vector dimensions: 2560
disabled generic openai-compatible document vector dimensions: 2560
Current head: 4d6adf6cdd28de1c23eb89b35111236b0fa5f622
Generated at: 2026-07-17T12:26:33.099Z
Configured model: Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B
```

Captured redacted request bodies:


**Observed result after fix:** Both provider paths returned 2560-dimensional vectors in enabled and disabled modes. Enabled query request bodies were prefixed with `Instruct: Given a user query, retrieve relevant memory notes and documents\nQuery:...`; disabled query request bodies stayed raw; document request bodies stayed raw in both modes.

**What was not tested:** Every OpenAI-compatible embedding server and model family was not tested. This proof covers the shared Qwen3 template behavior and the enabled/disabled contract for both affected provider paths.

## Root Cause (if applicable)

- Root cause: The OpenAI-compatible embedding paths did not have a shared, opt-in way to mirror the instruction-aware query-prefix handling already used by other memory embedding providers.
- Missing detection / guardrail: Unit tests did not verify provider-specific query payloads for instruction-aware models.
- Contributing context (if known): Some OpenAI-compatible servers expose embedding models that expect different query and document input formatting even when they use an OpenAI-style `/embeddings` API.

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

- Coverage level that should have caught this:
 - [x] Unit test
 - [ ] Seam / integration test
 - [ ] End-to-end test
 - [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient
- Target tests/files: `extensions/openai/embedding-provider.test.ts`, `src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts`, `src/agents/memory-search.test.ts`, and `src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts`.
- Scenario the tests should lock in: The opt-in flag propagates through memory-search provider creation; Qwen3/Mixedbread query embeddings include the expected query instruction prefix only when enabled; document batch embeddings and disabled/default queries remain raw.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: The behavior is local to provider request payload construction plus memory-search config propagation.
- Existing test that already covers this (if any): N/A
- If no new test is added, why not: N/A

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

OpenAI-compatible memory embedding providers can now opt into query instruction templates for known instruction-aware embedding models via `memorySearch.queryInstructionTemplate: true`. Defaults remain raw, and document embeddings are unchanged.

## Diagram (if applicable)

```text
Default:
[memory search query] -> [raw query embedding input]

Opt-in:
[memory search query] -> [model-specific query instruction prefix] -> [embedding input]

Documents:
[indexed memory/document] -> [raw document embedding input]
```

## Security Impact (required)

- New permissions/capabilities? (`Yes/No`) No
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? (`Yes/No`) No
- New/changed network calls? (`Yes/No`) No
- Command/tool execution surface changed? (`Yes/No`) No
- Data access scope changed? (`Yes/No`) No
- If any `Yes`, explain risk + mitigation: N/A

## Repro + Verification

### Environment

- OS: Linux
- Runtime/container: Local OpenClaw development checkout
- Model/provider: `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B` through an OpenAI-compatible loopback endpoint for exact request capture
- Integration/channel (if any): OpenClaw memorySearch provider construction and embedding provider adapters
- Relevant config (redacted): `memorySearch.queryInstructionTemplate: true` for enabled proof cases; omitted/false for disabled proof cases; endpoint port and API key redacted.

### Steps

1. Configure bundled OpenAI and generic `openai-compatible` memory embedding providers with `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B`.
2. Exercise query and document embedding calls with `queryInstructionTemplate: true`.
3. Exercise query and document embedding calls with `queryInstructionTemplate` disabled.
4. Compare captured `/v1/embeddings` request bodies.

### Expected

- Enabled query embeddings for Qwen3 include the shared query instruction prefix.
- Disabled/default query embeddings remain raw.
- Document embeddings are not query-prefixed.

### Actual

- Enabled query embeddings for both provider paths were prefixed as expected.
- Disabled query embeddings for both provider paths stayed raw.
- Document embedding payloads stayed raw in both modes.

## Evidence

Attach at least one:

- [x] Failing test/log before + passing after
- [x] Trace/log snippets
- [ ] Screenshot/recording
- [ ] Perf numbers (if relevant)

Verification run after the 2026-07-17 rebase/comment fix:

- `CI=true corepack pnpm test -- extensions/openai/embedding-provider.test.ts` - 1 file passed, 21 tests passed
- `CI=true corepack pnpm test -- src/plugins/openai-compatible-embedding-provider.test.ts` - 1 file passed, 36 tests passed
